newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Afghan Taleban's enemy Masood moves headquarters.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban's enemy Masood moves headquarters.

text.p: Ousted government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood has moved his headquarters out of his Panjsher Valley stronghold after Afghanistan's Islamist Taleban reached its gates, an Afghan news service said on Thursday.

The Pakistan-based Afghan Islamic Press (AIP) said Masood moved the headquarters to Andarab, between the valley and the Salang Pass cutting through the Hindu Kush, so he could defend the valley and attack the Taleban.
AIP said Masood had sent a 20-truck convoy with supplies to the new headquarters in Andarab on Wednesday. It was not immediately known what the trucks were carrying.

In the past two weeks, the Taleban have made a rapid push to the foothills of the Hindu Kush, some 100 km (60 miles) north of Kabul, re-occupying positions they held in October shortly after taking the Afghan capital.

At that time the black-turbanned fighters were driven back in part because of a rash of uprisings and ambushes at their rear and their commanders have made it clear the Taleban will not allow that to happen again.

They have told the mostly ethnic Tajik population suspected of loyalty to Masood to leave and are searching for weapons. Taleban officials have said the population will not be allowed back until the search is complete, but have not said how long it will take.
The Taleban have pushed up into the Salang Pass, which leads into the northern territory of Masood ally Abdul Rashid Dostum.
The alliance has set off explosions in the steep sides of the winding pass to bring down landslides to block the Taleban advance.
Masood set up similar barriers at the narrow mouth of the Panjsher Valley in October.

In the 1980s, when fighting a communist government backed by the Soviet Union, Masood's Tajik fighters frequently cut the Salang Pass and attacked convoys bringing war supplies down from Central Asia.
The Soviet army made frequent assaults on the Panjsher Valley, but never succeeded in holding it.

The Taleban, who have taken control of about two-thirds of the nation in two years since the movement was born in religious schools in refugee camps in Pakistan, is committed to bringing its stern version of Islam's Shariah law to the whole country.
